title: Synergistic experimental and ANN-based prediction of mechanical properties of basalt fiber reinforced high-strength concrete
abstract: Abstract This research focuses on how basalt macrofibers and microfibres affect the durability and Mechanical properties of M60 high-strength concrete. Compressive, split tensile, flexural strength, and acid resistance tests were employed to assess the performance of fiber-reinforced concrete at various fibre volume fractions. The findings demonstrate that the addition basalt fibres greatly enhanced the overall behaviour of concrete compared with the conventional control mix. The greatest compressive strengths were attained at a fibre dosage of 0.75%, reaching 68.42 MPa for microfibres and 63.86 MPa for macrofibres, compared to 58.81 MPa for conventional concrete. Additionally, split tensile strength increased as the fibre content increased to 0.75%, beyond which a slight reduction was observed, likely due to reduced matrix uniformity. Flexural performance showed substantial enhancement, with peak values of 8.78 and 7.88 MPa for microfibre- and macrofibre-reinforced concrete, respectively, demonstrating improved crack resistance and ductile behaviour. Durability evaluation through acid resistance testing revealed comparable performance at the optimum fibre dosage, although a marginal increase in weight loss was observed at higher fibre contents. Microstructural investigations confirmed effective fibre–matrix interaction and crack-bridging mechanisms, while XRD analysis verified the presence of stable crystalline phases that contributed to matrix integrity. Overall, basalt fibre reinforcement enhanced strength, toughness and durability characteristics of concrete. Furthermore, the experimental dataset was integrated with a model of an artificial neural network that accomplished high prediction accuracy. To validate and extend the predictive capability, additional Machine learning approaches were used, and strong agreement was shown with the experimental observations.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Concrete is widely used building material in civil engineering due to its low tensile strength, poor crack resistance, good compression strength, and limited energy absorption capacity. In addition to these advantages, high strength concrete has a number of disadvantages, such as increased brittleness and a reduced strain capacity, which is more obvious when compared to regular concrete, according to Cwirzen et al. [ 1 ]. According to Thong M. Pham [ 2 ], concrete composites’ flexural, tensile strength, impact resistance, post-cracking behaviour, and the ability to absorb energy is all enhanced by the inclusion of fibres. Many fibres, such as glass, steel, polypropylene, carbon, natural fibres have been widely researched, nevertheless, concerns about corrosion, durability, cost, and environmental impact have prompted researchers to investigate alternate fibre materials. In recent years, basalt fibre has received a lot of attention as a potential reinforcement material for high-strength concrete. Basalt fibres with remarkable modulus of elasticity, high tensile strength, great thermal stability, and superior chemical resistance are produced by melting naturally occurring basalt rock and extruding it into continuous filaments [ 3 ]. Basalt fibres have better alkali resistance in cementitious conditions than glass fibres and are non-corrosive, in contrast to steel fibres. Additionally, Basalt fibres are safe for the environment because they may be used in sustainable construction applications because their manufacture uses abundant natural raw materials and doesn’t require any additives [ 4 ]. Several experiments have demonstrated that, adding basalt fibres greatly enhances its mechanical qualities. Because of efficient crack-bridging mechanisms, Pereira de Oliveira et al. [ 5 ] found significant increases in the flexural and tensile strengths when basalt fibres are used as reinforcement. Previous research has demonstrated that the addition of basalt fibre improves the concrete’s structural performance. Improved load-carrying capacity and a change in the failure behaviour concrete reinforced with basalt fibres from brittle fracture to a more ductile reaction were seen in research by Kearley and Bui [ 6 ]. The effectiveness of the fibre reinforcement is mostly determined by a number of variables, including the fibre aspect ratio, dosage, and the consistency of the fibre distribution within the cementitious matrix [ 7 ]. According to research by Uratsinze et al. [ 8 ], basalt fibre can function well in terms of workability and mechanical qualities when its volume is varied between 0.3 and 0.6 percent also the basalt fibres enhance concrete’s durability in addition to its mechanical qualities. Fibre incorporation improves resistance to harsh environmental conditions like chemical exposure, freeze–thaw action, and chloride ingress by reducing permeability, limiting water absorption, and controlling crack development, according to Mattei & Piccininni et al., [ 9 ]. Additionally, according to Samiha Tasneem et al. [ 10 ], adding basalt fibre to concrete combined with other cementitious materials improves its sustainability and long-term durability. Kumar Mohit et al., [ 11 ] employed a new model of artificial neural networks that was enhanced using the slime mould method and opposition-based learning. The fibre sandwiched structures displayed the greatest tensile strength, which were confirmed using a hybrid slime mould method and ANN model. Applying the machine learning (ML) methods, Mir Muaviz Saleem et al. [ 12 ] predicted the dimensional correctness and tolerance of the geometric features. The primary objective in the field of ML is to program systems to automatically learn from data and develop by experience. Machine learning strategies require a large amount of data to provide predictions. Mohit Kumar et al., [ 13 ] analysed the tensile stress in ABS/Glass fibre composite materials was predicted using the machine learning technique, In addition to utilising machine learning techniques to predict bearing response in hydrothermally aged epoxy composite reinforced with carbon-fiber joints, The model is evaluated by performance indicators such as R-squared, mean absolute deviation (MAD), and squared root mean error (RMSE). Sharma H et al., [ 14 ] used the concepts of ML to forecast the mechanical characteristics of composite material. Several ML methods, including K-nearest neighbours, random forest(RF), and extreme gradient boosting was used in forecasting these characteristics. Among these, the RF model was the most reliable and accurate, especially for polypropylene/carbon nanotubes composites. The RF model outperformed compared to other methods. The study on forecasting thermoplastic nanocomposites was further extended, yielding a high coefficient of determination of 0.9875 and low values of 0.0228, 0.0189, and 0.0005 for root mean square error, mean absolute error, and mean square error, respectively. The homogenisation of elastic properties under quasi-static loading using BC’s that were periodic accomplished using an FFT-based approach by Maninder Pal Singh et al., [ 15 ]. The numerical and DIGIMAT results showed a high degree of agreement. In order to forecast material properties and solve issues like data quality and model interpretability, Sharma H et al., [ 16 ] employed a variety of ML techniques, which ultimately supported advances in composite materials research and development. Yashas G. T. et al. [ 17 ] investigated the hybrid composites with carbon fibre and basalt fiber as reinforcement. According to the results, the composites produced in this work is applicable to a number of engineering medium load applications in structural engineering in the future. Changfa Zhou et al., [ 18 ] reported improved energy absorption and impact resistance of BFRC, appropriate for buildings subject to seismic loads, vibrations and repeated loading. Despite the fact that there has a lot of progress in comprehending the benefits of concrete with basalt fibre as reinforcement, more systematic study is required to completely characterise its effectiveness when paired with high-strength concrete matrices. Based on the literature, variations in fibre geometry, dose, concrete grade, and curing circumstances can lead to inconsistent results. In order to develop reliable design concepts for basalt fibre reinforced high-strength concrete, thorough performance studies covering mechanical strength, durability behaviour, and failure mechanisms are crucial.

In this regard, the present research uses a thorough experimental examination to evaluate the performance characteristics of high-strength concrete with basalt fibre reinforcement. In order to advance sustainable, long-lasting and high performing concrete materials for infrastructure applications, the research focuses on evaluating the impact of basalt fibre addition on flexural behaviour, compressive, tensile strength and overall structural performance.

sections.heading: Standard portland cement (OPC 53 grade)
paragraphs: The main binder utilised in this investigation was grade 53 ordinary Portland cement, which conforms with IS 12269. For high-strength concrete, OPC 53 grade cement is recommended because of its greater early and final strength development. The cement was suitable for M60 grade high-performance concrete (HPC) since it demonstrated good fineness, consistency, and setting time characteristics. In the investigation, grade 53 Birla ordinary cement was utilised. As shown in Fig.  1 a to e, the relative gravity of the cement discovered to be 3.0 based on physical analysis. sections.heading: Coarse and fine aggregate
paragraphs: Manufactured sand (M-sand) served as the fine aggregate that complied with Zone II of IS 383. When compared to natural sand, M-sand offers improved particle form, grading control, and fewer contaminants. In high-strength concrete, the angular shape and rough texture of M-sand improve mechanical performance and interfacial bonding. As seen in Fig.  1 , the fine aggregate utilised in this investigation can go through a 4.75-mm sieve and meet conventional grading requirements for the manufacturing of concrete. This material was locally sourced from surrounding areas, ensuring practical relevance and reducing transportation-related environmental impacts. The coarse aggregate, which are of 12 and 20 mm in size used in this investigation. The aggregate was clean, well-graded, and free from deleterious materials. Coarse aggregate is essential to strength development and dimensional stability of high-strength concrete, particularly in fiber-reinforced systems. Utilisation of indigenous materials complies with environmentally friendly building methods while maintaining cost-effectiveness.

sections.heading: Chemical admixture
paragraphs: Conplast SP430, a super plasticising ingredient, is used to reduce water usage in concrete mixtures. According to BS 5075, ASTM C 494 Type A and Type F and BS: EN 934–2, the brown liquid possesses a specific gravity of 1.18. Increasing workability, decreasing bleeding and segregation, and enhancing cohesion and particle dispersion are all benefits of this superplasticizer. The primary aim of its utilisation in the investigation was to lower the water content without compromising workability. Conplast SP 430 has been employed to achieve the required workability and generate high-strength concrete with an appropriate cement and water content. In the investigation, it was discovered to enhance the concrete’s workability without requiring additional water. The super plasticiser dosage remained constant throughout the experiment. It was added at a dose proportion of 0.1% of weight of the binder.

sections.heading: Fibres of basalt
paragraphs: Melting silica-rich igneous basalt rock at temperatures between 1450 and 1500 °C produces basalt fibres. After that, the molten substance is pulled through small nozzles to form continuous filaments has a 10–20 µm diameter. Compared to many synthetic fibre production processes, this one is easier to use and more ecologically beneficial because no additives are needed. The resulting fibres are in two groups based on thickness: macro fibres, which are thicker and utilised in structural applications needing high strength and load-bearing capacity, improved post-cracking behavior and energy absorption, and micro fibres, which are incredibly fine and employed to control micro-crack initiation and propagation. These varieties are safer substitutes for asbestos due to their small diameters and great tensile strength, chemical resistance, and durability.

Basalt fibres are extensively utilised in concrete reinforcing, woven textiles, and filament winding (such as in CNG cylinders). Because of its superior mechanical performance and resistance to corrosion, basalt fibre reinforced polymer (BFRP) rebars are one cutting-edge application that can replace conventional steel reinforcement. To investigate their impact on mechanical, durability, and microstructural performance, the fibres shown in Fig.  2 a and b were added in volume fractions of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1%. sections.heading: Design of high-performance concrete mixes and fibre content
paragraphs: Design of mix for M60 grade high-performance concrete was carried out in line with IS 10262 and relevant guidelines for HPC. To ensure that M60 concrete has the appropriate strength and durability, a low water-to-cement ratio was used in the design of the blend. The superplasticizer dose was carefully adjusted to preserve sufficient workability while maintaining the mix’s mechanical performance. As illustrated in Table  3 , basalt fibres in both micro and macro forms were incorporated into the reference mix at volume fractions of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1.0%. The control mix exhibited the most slump, and as the proportion of basalt fibre grew, workability steadily decreased. Nonetheless, by enhancing particle dispersion and compensating for the loss of flowability, the use of a superplasticizer maintained adequate consistency for casting and compaction. Basalt fibres increased cohesion and reduced segregation and bleeding by forming a reinforcing network inside the matrix, increasing the yield stress and plastic viscosity of the concrete. Since too much fibre addition may have a detrimental effect on workability, proper mix design and uniform fibre distribution are essential. A high-performance water-reducing ingredient and rigorous mixing processes ensured consistent fibre dispersion while maintaining acceptable fresh concrete properties. Following mixing, each specimen was cast, compacted, and cured before testing under typical laboratory conditions. Table 3 Conventional mix proportions Sl. sections.heading: Specimen casting
paragraphs: The casting of specimens utilised in this investigation is depicted in Fig.  3 a to d. The mixture was poured in 150*150*150 mm sample to inspect the concrete’s compressive strength. Similarly, dimensions of 100*100*500 mm were filled to evaluate the bending strength and specimens with dimensions of 150 and 300 mm in diameter and length respectively were employed to evaluate the tensile strength. Nine cubes and nine cylinders using M40-grade regular concrete were cast for this study. Additionally, in 27 cubes and 27 cylinders, basalt fibre was utilised instead of cement at percentages of 0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1%. The concrete moulds were immersed in water to cure for seven, fourteen, and twenty-eight days. Each blend includes three sets of specimens were prepared. After testing, the three specimens’ average value was considered. Fig. 3 a  to  d  Shows specimen and curing

Durability test
paragraphs: Performance in terms of durability was assessed using acid attack tests. The specimens were made from cube moulds of 150*150*150 mm. For acid resistance evaluation, the curing water was supplemented with 15% sulphuric acid. The specimens are removed after curing process and are allowed to dry for one day, cleaned properly, and then subjected to testing. To assess resistance to harsh chemical conditions, both the % of weight loss and a decrease in compressive strength were computed. The effectiveness of the basalt fibres in improving durability was assessed by comparing the performance of fiber-reinforced concrete.

sections.heading: Result and discussions
paragraphs: The outcomes of the investigation were evaluated in detail in this section. The mechanical qualities of concrete containing both macro and micro basalt fibres were examined and contrasted so as to ascertain their individual effectiveness along with their overall contribution to strength growth and performance behaviour.

sections.heading: Concrete compressive strength with macro and micro basalt fibre
paragraphs: The M60 grade concrete’s compressive strength with different percentage of macro and micro basalt fibres is displayed in Fig.  5 ; a consistent upward trend is seen with increasing fibre dose. After 28 days, the strength increased from 58.81 MPa (control mix) to 68.42 MPa for micro fiber-reinforced concrete and from 58.81 MPa to 63.86 MPa for macro fiber-reinforced concrete with varying basalt fibre percentages. These values satisfy IS-516’s requirements as well as IS 10262’s mix design criteria. The achieved 28-day strengths for M60 grade concrete exceed the planned mean strength, demonstrating the efficacy and sufficiency of the chosen mix design. The compressive strength enhancement that has been noted can be attributed to a number of factors as the basalt fibres enhances the internal matrix structure by preventing microcracks from developing and spreading. Fig. 5 Compression strength v/s percentage of micro and macro-Basalt fiber

Specifically, under compressive loading, micro basalt fibres efficiently regulate early-age shrinkage cracking, leading to a denser matrix and more consistent stress transfer. In order to prevent abrupt brittle failure and delay crack coalescence, macro fibres help bridge bigger cracks. The interaction between the fibre and matrix increases compressive capacity by reducing internal stresses and enhancing load transmission efficiency. These outcomes are close with current journal research [ 19 ,  20 ] that demonstrate how basalt fibre reinforcement improves high-strength concrete’s ductility, compressive strength, and crack resistance by reducing porosity and improving interfacial bonding. The best results at 0.75% fibre concentration indicate that this dosage effectively bridges cracks without seriously impairing workability or leading to fibre clustering. Excessive fibre addition may limit additional strength improvement by reducing compaction efficiency and creating voids.

sections.heading: Split tensile strength with macro and micro basalt fibre
paragraphs: The substantial impact of fibre dosage on tensile performance at 28 days is demonstrated by the tensile test results of M60 concrete reinforcing with macro and micro basalt fibres displayed in Fig.  6 . Concrete is prone to brittle breaking and is intrinsically weak in tension, hence tensile strength is crucial. Tensile strength of micro fibre specimens rose from 4.46 MPa (0%) to 6.23 MPa at 0.75% after 28 days, and subsequently steadily decreased with increasing fibre dosages. This decrease is attributable to the formation of voids, decreased workability, and fibre clustering, all of which weaken the zone of interfacial transition and impair the efficiency of stress transfer. Similarly, strength of macro fibre specimen rose from 4.46 MPa (0%) to 5.23 MPa at 0.75%. According to this pattern, a moderate fibre content improves tensile stress redistribution and crack-bridging, while larger concentrations decrease matrix coherence and bonding effectiveness. Similar findings were documented in Zhang et al. [ 20 ], where an excess of basalt fibre led to reduced tensile strength because of the increased porosity and insufficient fibre dispersion. Fig. 6 Tensile strength v/s percentage of micro and macro-Basalt fiber

In comparison to macro fiber-reinforced concrete, specimens utilising micro basalt fibres demonstrated a more consistent and uniform increase in compressive strength. Concrete reinforced with micro and macro fibres demonstrated strength gains of 32.46 and 13.20%, respectively, after 28 days. Because they can stop microcracks from forming and spreading, microfibres work better by improving the way stress is distributed throughout the cementitious matrix. At modest fibre contents, microfibres enhance matrix integrity without significantly lowering workability. These findings support the conclusions given by Kumar and Singh [ 21 ]. Furthermore, Alnahhal et al. [ 22 ] indicated that optimal fibre contents in the range of 0.25–0.5% provide greatest gains in tensile performance, but excessive fibre addition may result in agglomeration, lowering the efficiency of fibre reinforcement and overall mechanical performance. Overall, the outcomes show that basalt fibres positively influence tensile performance, particularly at optimum concentrations. Micro fibres exhibit more stable and effective improvement due to better dispersion and crack control.

sections.heading: Flexural strength with macro and micro basalt fibre
paragraphs: The M60 grade concrete’s 28-day flexural strength results incorporating micro and macro basalt fibres shown in Fig.  7  demonstrate the significant impact of the type of fibre and dosage on bending performance. For micro fibre-reinforced specimens, a gradual and consistent enhance in flexural strength is noticed with enhancing fibre content to 0.75%. The control mixes exhibited strength of 5.25 MPa, which increased to a maximum of 8.78 MPa at 0.75% fibre dosage. The percentage increased in flexural strength was 39.86%. Fig. 7 Flexural strength v/s percentage of micro and macro-Basalt fiber

The improvement in flexural strength is caused by micro basalt fibres’ capacity to disperse stresses, stop microcrack formation, and strengthen the cement matrix. By bridging small cracks early in the loading process, microfibres improve load carrying capacity and delay their propagation. Similar results were reported by Kumar and Singh [ 21 ], who noted that microfibres provide more consistent flexural performance because to their effective crack-control capabilities. At 1.0% fibre concentration, strength reduced,this is due to a weaker fiber-matrix link, poor fibre dispersion, and decreased workability. Flexural strength, however, increased dramatically at 0.50 and 0.75% fibre concentrations, peaking at 8.78 MPa at 0.75%. By bridging broader cracks under bending loads, macro basalt fibres increased flexural strength by 33.33%, improving toughness, post-cracking resistance, ductility, and energy absorption capacity. Zhang et al., [ 20 ] confirms that higher macro basalt fibre content enhances flexural strength and post-crack behaviour due to improved pull-out resistance and crack-bridging mechanisms. Additionally, Alnahhal et al., [ 22 ] indicate that optimum macro fibre content significantly increases modulus of rupture, whereas insufficient or poorly distributed fibres may negatively influence performance due to reduced matrix continuity. Overall, the results demonstrate that 0.75% micro fibre addition is an effective way in maximizing M60 concrete’s flexural strength after 28 days.

sections.heading: Microstructural analysis
paragraphs: The microstructural features of high-performance concrete with basalt fibre were investigated using SEM. Fibre dispersion, fibre–matrix interfacial bonding, matrix densification and crack bridging techniques were seen in all samples taken from testing materials. The SEM analysis of basalt fibre concrete is displayed in Fig.  8 a to d. The phases may be distinguished clearly through lighter and darker areas because to the contrast seen in the microstructural pictures, which reflect changes in composition and surface topography. The photos show three main characteristics: hydration products, micro basalt fibres, and unreacted cement particles. Particularly apparent in Fig.  8 b, the unreacted cement particles are comparatively big, blocky, or irregularly shaped formations. The background matrix, which is made up of finer particles and typically appears amorphous or irregular, is formed by the surrounding cementitious hydration products. Furthermore, it is clear from Fig.  8 c & d that the micro basalt fibres are thin, thread-like, or needle-shaped structures. A specific degree of mechanical bridging and interlocking inside the matrix is indicated by the existence of these fibres and its interactions with the surrounding hydration products. This interaction strengthens the connection between fibre and the matrix, which greatly enhances concrete’s tensile strength and fracture resistance, especially following compressive loading. The images’ scale bars (such as 2, 5, and 10 µm) draw attention to the tiny microstructural details, like the fiber-matrix interface area and the shape of hydration products. These conclusions align with the fibre reinforcing process, which improves the material’s overall mechanical performance by using basalt fibres to stop, bend, or bridge micro cracks that normally cause brittle failure in concrete. Fig. 8 a  to  d  SEM examination of basalt fibre concrete’s microstructural topography and morphology

sections.heading: XRD analysis
paragraphs: The intense diffraction peak at roughly 26.6° (2θ) in the XRD of the basalt fiber concrete depicted in Fig.  9  indicates the existence of many crystalline phases, with quartz being the dominating phase. The appearance of additional peaks corresponding to anorthite and calcium aluminosilicate phases indicates that persistent hydration products are being produced inside the cementitious matrix. The increased intensity of these peaks suggests that the addition of basalt fibre enhances crystallinity and matrix densification. The preponderance of calcium aluminosilicate phases and the reduction of several hydration-sensitive peaks also suggest enhanced hydration and pozzolanic activity, which enhance mechanical performance. The formation of favourable crystalline phases and their role in improving the microstructural characteristics of basalt fiber-reinforced concrete are often highlighted by the XRD data. The absence of observable peaks that correspond to normal cement hydration results, such as ettringite, portlandite (Ca(OH)₂), and calcium silicate hydrate (CSH), is one significant finding. In bulk concrete XRD studies, the stronger peaks of crystalline minerals frequently obscure the diffraction signals from amorphous or weakly crystalline phases. Specifically, the main binding phase of hydrated cement, the CSH gel, is mostly amorphous and lacks identifiable diffraction peaks. As a result, rather than offering a thorough depiction of the cement gel structure, the acquired XRD pattern mostly depicts the mineralogical composition of the crystalline elements, such as aggregates and unreacted basalt-based materials or clinker phases. Fig.9 X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern of basalt fiber concrete

sections.heading: Crack failure behaviour of concrete specimens
paragraphs: The patterns of crack failure seen when concrete specimens were mechanically tested, as shown in Figs.  10 ,  11 ,  12 , clearly show how fibre reinforcing has a major impact on concrete’s failure behaviour and crack propagation characteristics. Failure was typically abrupt and brittle in conventional or regular concrete specimens. The primary cause of this behaviour is plain concrete’s inadequate strain tolerance and intrinsic low tensile capacity. Stress concentration around aggregates and pores causes internal microcracks to form under increasing load circumstances. These fractures quickly combine into a large crack, causing an unexpected failure with little warning. Nevertheless, inclusion of fibres in tests of flexural, split tensile, and compressive strengths to the concrete matrix significantly changed the failure mode, cracking mechanism, and overall structural response. Normal concrete specimens showed typical brittle crushing during the compressive test is dipicted in Fig.  10 a to b, which is characterised by abrupt crack formation and quick specimen disintegration once the peak force was reached. Explosive failure resulted from vertical cracks that started close to the mid-height area and swiftly spread to the loaded surfaces. An abrupt decrease of load-carrying capability resulted from the lack of reinforcing to prevent interior microcracks from growing. Fiber reinforced concrete specimens, however, in contrast, showed a more controlled and slow breakdown mechanism. By acting as crack arresters, the fibres dispersed throughout the cementitious matrix successfully postponed the start of cracks and limited their expansion. Improved stress redistribution within The specimen was revealed by a number of tiny cracks that developed gradually rather than a single prominent crack. The fibres improved post-peak load resistance and added resistance against fracture opening by bridging over emerging cracks. Fig.10 Cube specimens’ compression test failure mode Fig.11 Cylinder specimens’ split tensile test failure mode Fig.12 Beam specimens’ flexural test failure mode

Consequently, the fibre reinforced specimens depicted improved capacity for energy absorption and ductility than regular concrete, preserving the structural integrity even after apparent fissures formed. During the split tensile strength test, where tensile stresses are the primary cause of failure, the advantageous effect of fibres became even more apparent. When tensile stress above the concrete’s tensile capacity, normal concrete specimens under diametral compression showed instantaneous splitting along the vertical diameter. The specimen split into two halves abruptly and cleanly as the crack spread strongly from the centre toward both loading edges as seen in Fig.  11 a. The brittleness of ordinary concrete during circumstances of tensile loading is confirmed by this behaviour. Fiber-reinforced concrete specimens, However, in contrast, had smaller cracks and delayed crack start as viewed in Fig.  11 b. The fibres transferred tensile loads across crack planes by acting as micro-reinforcement elements through bonding and frictional resistance. The specimen did not split immediately because the fibres retained some of the tensile strain long after the break occurred. It wasn’t until the fibre gradually pulled out or burst and the crack expanded more steadily and slowly that it completely collapsed. This approach significantly increased the concrete’s toughness and tensile resistance. The fact that fiber-reinforced specimens have fewer cracks indicates how well fibres reduce brittle fracture behaviour while improving tensile performance. Similarly, the flexural test revealed that regular concrete and fiber-reinforced concrete had significantly different failure characteristics. Flexural stress in plain concrete beams caused tensile strains at the bottom fibre, resulting in crack initiation in the tension zone. As soon as the crack appeared, it quickly spread upward toward the compression zone, resulting in an instantaneous failure with little deformation as shown in Fig.  12 a. The load–deflection response showed minimal post-cracking resistance and a restricted energy absorption capability. Conversely, fibre-reinforced concrete beams showed several dispersed microcracks as shown in Fig.  12 . (b) rather than a single main crack. The specimen was able to support weight even after the initial fracture because the fibres significantly improved its capacity to bridge cracks. By reducing fracture opening and promoting more effective load redistribution by distributing stresses over the crack surfaces, the fibres postponed failure. Instead of breaking suddenly, the fissures gradually widened as force increased, demonstrating greater ductility and flexural toughness. Additionally, the reduction in fracture width and spacing contributed to the concrete elements’ enhanced resistance and longer service life. The change in failure behaviour from brittle to quasi-ductile is a significant outcome of fibre integration. Fiber-reinforced concrete exhibits incremental fracture propagation and observable deformation before to failure, as opposed to ordinary concrete, which collapses abruptly and without warning. This better behaviour promotes structural safety by providing a warning prior to collapse. The fibres also provide increased residual strength, toughness, and impact resistance after peak loading. Reduced crack breadth and frequency improve durability by preventing water and aggressive compounds from penetrating, lowering the risk of long-term degradation and corrosion of the reinforcement. These characteristics make fiber-reinforced concrete which is suitable for structures that must withstand severe environmental conditions and heavy service loads (Table  4 ). sections.heading: Modelling of artificial neural network
paragraphs: In this study, the mechanical qualities of basalt fiber reinforced concrete containing macro and micro fibres were modelled and predicted using Artificial Neural Networks (ANNs), an advanced machine learning technique. The behaviour of fiber-reinforced concrete is particularly nonlinear because to the complex interactions between fibre dose, curing age, matrix characteristics, and fibre-matrix bonding. It is often challenging for traditional statistical and analytical models to accurately depict these relationships. ANNs, which are architecture based and behaviour of biological neural networks, provide a powerful data-driven framework for learning detailed patterns from experimental data and producing accurate forecasts of concrete performance. The proposed ANN model, shown in Fig.  13 , includes an input layer, hidden computational layers, and an output layer connected by weighted neurones. The input components that are considered, include the kind of fibre (macro and micro), the percentage of fibre (0.25, 0.5, 0.75, and 1%), the curing age (7, 14, and 28 days), and the water binder ratio. The data include concrete’s flexural, split tensile, and compressive strengths. A feed-forward backpropagation neural network design was chosen to replicate complex nonlinear interactions between material variables and strength parameters. Three output neurones representing flexural strength, split tensile strength, and compressive strength, five input neurones, twelve neurones in the first hidden layer, and ten neurones in the second hidden layer made up the network. Because of its powerful nonlinear mapping capabilities and adaptive learning behaviour, ANN models outperform traditional statistical methods in predicting tangible features [ 23 ,  24 ]. The output layer employed a linear (purelin) activation function suitable for continuous strength prediction, but the hidden layer used the tangent sigmoid (tansig) activation function to efficiently capture nonlinear behaviour. The network was trained at a learning rate of 0.001 using the Adam optimisation method to achieve efficient and consistent convergence. To achieve the best learning performance, a batch size of eight and a total of 150 epochs were used. To increase model performance and avoid bias induced by different data scales, each input and output set of data was normalised using Min–Max scaling. The dataset was divided as follows: 70% for training, 15% for validation, and 15% for testing. The model’s performance was evaluated using the root mean square error (RMSE), mean absolute error(MAE), and coefficient of determination(R2). Table  5  shows a 24-trial experimental design matrix representing the ANN model’s training and validation dataset. Neural networks can learn the combined impact of material parameters on strength increase because the information includes variations in fibre type, dosage, curing time, and water-binder ratio. The studies demonstrate that compressive, tensile, and flexural strengths progressively enhances with curing time for both macro and micro basalt fibres. This trend is driven mostly by the cement’s continual hydration and the gradual densification of the ITZ between the cement matrix and fibres. While macro fibres act as crack-bridging components, increasing post-cracking load carrying capacity and toughness, micro basalt fibres effectively limit the formation of microcracks during early loading phases, hence increasing tensile resistance. Sim et al. [ 25 ] observed similar gains in fibre-reinforced concrete, showing that basalt fibres improve stress transmission across fissures, increasing ductility and fracture resistance. In line with the ANN model, during 28-day curing circumstances, Compressive strength peaks performance at roughly 0.68% micro fibre and 0.62% macro fibre content. Similarly, the range of 0.72%–0.82% fibre content was where tensile and flexural strengths performed at their best. These outcomes indicate that workability and fibre dispersion are not greatly impacted, moderate fibre addition maximises mechanical efficiency by enhancing crack resistance. Asteris and Mokos [ 26 ] had comparable outcomes, indicating that ANN models efficiently estimate ideal concrete mix parameters while reducing experimental trials. The created ANN model’s prediction reliability is assessed by the training and validation performance charts in Fig.  14 . The high degree of agreement between the actual and expected strength values in the validation curves indicates that network learning was successful. The model avoided overfitting and retained its capacity to generalise to new data, as evidenced by its quick training convergence and reliable validation behaviour. The small prediction error across compressive, tensile, and flexural strength outputs suggests that the ANN was effective in capturing correlations between curing age, fibre dosage, and matrix characteristics. As illustrated in Fig.  15 , the developed model’s reliability is proven by comparing experimental results to ANN-generated predictions. The expected results closely match the observed patterns for all mechanical parameters tested, indicating a high level of prediction accuracy. The intrinsic heterogeneity of concrete materials, uneven fibre distribution, and potential errors during specimen casting and testing processes could all contribute to small discrepancies between the measured and estimated values. However, the forecast errors continue to be below acceptable engineering tolerances, demonstrating the ANN technique’s durability and efficacy. Previous studies on ANN applications for high-performance and fiber-reinforced concrete systems, which also recorded equivalent prediction performance, have shown the value of artificial intelligence techniques in predicting the behaviour of construction materials [ 27 ]. The correlation between curing age and fibre percentage on mechanical qualities is graphically shown by a three-dimensional response surface diagrams in Fig.  16 . The response surfaces clearly show nonlinear strength development patterns, where strength improves with fibre addition up to an optimal range and rises with curing time as a result of hydration progression. Strength enhancement tends to stabilise beyond this range, indicating the existence of an ideal fibre dosage. Additionally, the surfaces demonstrate that tensile and flexural performance is more affected by fibre reinforcement than compressive strength, which is consistent with fibres’ ability to bridge cracks. These visual aids facilitate intelligent concrete mixture optimisation and help researchers comprehend parameter sensitivity. Response surface analysis integrated with ANN modelling has suggested for complex material systems where multiple interacting parameters govern performance [ 28 ]. The performance evaluation metrics of the created ANN model for forecasting the flexural, split tensile and compressive strength of M60 concrete strengthened using basalt fibre are shown in Fig.  17 a to c. Three statistical measures were adopted in order to find the model’s performance such as RMSE, MAE, and R 2 . For each of the three mechanical attributes, R 2  values displayed in Fig.  17 a demonstrate exceptional prediction accuracy. Tensile strength (0.987), flexural strength (0.981), and compressive strength (0.992) were the models with the greatest R 2  values. The ANN model shows a significant connection between the expected and experimental findings because all values are extremely close to unity, demonstrating its ability to correctly capture the nonlinear interactions within the dataset. The average magnitude of prediction mistakes is shown by the MAE values as in Fig.  17 b. MAE values of 0.63 MPa for compressive strength, 0.05 MPa for split tensile strength, and 0.08 MPa for flexural strength were produced with the ANN model. Reliable predictive performance is demonstrated by these low error values, which show that the differences between expected and actual measurements are negligible. In a similar vein, the RMSE values confirm the model’s efficacy as seen in Fig.  17 c. Compressive, split tensile, and flexural strength had RMSE values of 0.91, 0.08, and 0.12 MPa, respectively. The relatively lower value of RMSE states that the ANN model is considerable generalisation capacity and maintains great prediction accuracy across a range of strength attributes. sections.heading: Statistical analysis
paragraphs: The compressive, split tensile, and flexural strength data of M60 basalt fibre-reinforced concrete were statistically evaluated to determine the reliability of the experimental findings. For each testing circumstance, the reported strength value is the average of three specimens tested under the same conditions. The data’s dispersion was found using standard deviation (SD) and coefficient of variation. Furthermore, ANOVA was used to investigate the effect of various fibre doses on measured strengths. The null hypothesis assumes no significant difference between the mean strengths of the various concrete mixtures. A significance level of 0.05 was used, and differences were judged statistically significant when the p-value was less than 0.05.

The statistical analysis demonstrated that, the addition of basalt fibres resulted in measurable improvements in compressive, split tensile, and flexural strengths. The low standard deviation and coefficient of variation values indicate that the experimental results are consistent and reproducible, and the confidence intervals contribute to the dependability of the observed strengths. The ANOVA results in Table  7  show that fibre integration provides statistically significant benefits. These findings show that the experimental dataset is stable and serve as a solid foundation for future ML predictions. sections.heading: Comparative evaluation of machine learning models
paragraphs: To determine the effectiveness of the developed Artificial Neural Network (ANN), its predictive performance was contrasted to several ML algorithms, such as Linear Regression (LR), Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbours (KNN), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Gradient Boosting. The models were tested to predict the mechanical properties of basalt fiber reinforced concrete using common performance indicators such as coefficient of determination (R 2 ) and root mean square error (RMSE). The comparison study evaluates each algorithm’s accuracy, dependability, and generalisation capabilities, showing the benefits of the suggested ANN model over other ML methodologies. To forecast the mechanical characteristics of basalt fiber concrete, Fig.  18  a to c compares the effectiveness of different machine learning methods and optimises combinations of basalt fibres. The R 2  values from six machine learning algorithms; LR, RF, GB, DT, KNN, and SVR are compared in Fig.  18 a. The R2 score shows how much of the experimental data’s variation is covered by the model; values nearer one suggests higher predictive accuracy. With an R2 value that was close to 0.99, Linear Regression had the highest R2 value among the models that were assessed, indicating a high degree of association between anticipated and actual results. While Decision Tree showed somewhat lesser accuracy, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting also showed outstanding prediction ability with R 2  values near 0.90. KNN and SVR’s R 2  values were significantly lower, indicating that they had a harder time capturing the intricate connections between the characteristics of concrete strength and the input parameters. Figure  18 b displays the RMSE values for the same machine learning models. Fig. 18 a  to  c  Comparative analysis of various ML algorithms using the best Basalt fibre combination, R 2  value, and RMSE

Better model performance is indicated by lower RMSE values, which quantify the average prediction error. The best prediction ability was confirmed by the fact that Linear Regression had the lowest RMSE value. Additionally, Random Forest and Gradient Boosting showed comparatively low RMSE values, suggesting accurate forecasts. KNN and SVR, on the other hand, generated greater RMSE values, indicating greater differences between the experimental and projected outcomes. The agreement between the R2 and RMSE investigations indicates that Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Gradient Boosting are the best models to forecast the mechanical qualities of basalt fiber concrete. The optimised basalt fibre combinations and the accompanying estimated compressive strengths are displayed in Fig.  18 c. Based on the findings, fibre combinations with larger percentages of macro and micro basalt fibres typically demonstrated superior performance in strength. Mixes containing roughly 0.75% micro fibre and 0.75% macro fibre had the highest anticipated compressive strength between the combinations under investigation, with values above 72 MPa. The optimised combinations show that a proper ratio of micro to macro fibres increases stress distribution, strength growth, and crack-bridging mechanisms. These results demonstrate how well hybrid basalt fibre reinforcement improves the mechanical properties of high-strength concrete.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The following results were reached in view of the experimental study: The use of basalt fibres enhanced the mechanical properties of M60 grade high-performance concrete. Following 28 days of curing with 0.75% of micro basalt fibre, the greatest compressive and split tensile strengths were attained, with an enhance of 16.34% in compressive strength and 32.46% in tensile strength. Similarly, 8.58 and 13.20% improvement in the compression and tensile strengths respectively for macro basalt fibre. Similarly, the strength of flexure after 28 days of cure for micro basalt fibre was 39.86 and 33.33% for Macro basalt fibre. The maximum strength was seen for micro basalt fibre at dosage of 0.75%. Basalt fibre-reinforced concrete demonstrated enhanced durability performance because it is more resistance to acid attack. SEM investigation verified efficient crack-bridging processes and robust fibre-matrix interfacial bonding. The strength, hardness, and high-strength concrete’s durability were enhanced by inclusion of micro and macro basalt fibres. According to the results, addition of fibres to concrete greatly improves its compressive, split tensile, and flexural performance by decreasing the spread of cracks, increasing ductility, and altering the mode of failure from abrupt brittle fracture to a more gradual and controlled failure behaviour. From ANN Technique, it was also observed that the experimental results and ANN results are inline and the optimized parameters are same as experimental work with least error. The optimisation analysis revealed that the basalt fibre combination of 0.75% micro fibre and 0.75% macro fibre was the most efficient mix for increasing the compressive strength of high-strength concrete, while the comparative evaluation of ML algorithms demonstrated that with the highest R 2  value, linear regression produced the best predicted accuracy. and lowest RMSE value.
